\chapter{Sorry}
\label{ch:te-sorry}
\hlchaptermodality{9}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can apologise in Telugu and ask someone to forgive me, using the same respectful ending.}

Say \te{క్షమించండి}, unpack it as kṣamin̄cu plus the respectful -aṇḍi already met in kūrcōṇḍi, and trace it to Sanskrit kṣamā.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kṣamin̄caṇḍi]{\te{క్షమించండి} — sorry}

\label{lesson:TE-C09-kshaminchandi}



\begin{quote}
You already know \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} and its respectful \textbf{‑\te{ండి}} ending (\emph{kūrcōṇḍi}, \textquotedblleft{}please sit\textquotedblright{}). Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} hands you that very ending again, riding a brand-new verb.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{క్షమా}} (\emph{kṣamā}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{forgiveness, patience}\textquotedblright{} — the Sanskrit noun, borrowed whole.
  \item \textbf{‑\te{ఇంచు}} (\emph{‑in̄cu}) = a \textbf{verb-making suffix}: \emph{kṣamā} + \emph{‑in̄cu} $\to$ \textbf{\te{క్షమించు}} (\emph{kṣamin̄cu}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to forgive}.\textquotedblright{} (The same pattern gives \te{ప్రారంభించు} \emph{prārambhin̄cu}, \textquotedblleft{}to begin,\textquotedblright{} from Sanskrit \emph{prārambha}.)
  \item \textbf{‑\te{ండి}} (\emph{‑aṇḍi}) = the \textbf{respectful imperative} ending — exactly the one you already met on \emph{kūrcōṇḍi} \textquotedblleft{}please sit\textquotedblright{} and \emph{ceppaṇḍi} \textquotedblleft{}please tell me.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{please forgive}\textquotedblright{} — the same polite mold you already know, filled with a new verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Telugu \textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} \emph{kṣamin̄\textbf{caṇḍi}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣamā} + \textbf{‑in̄cu} (verb) + \textbf{‑aṇḍi} (imperative)
  \item Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ}} \emph{kṣami\textbf{si}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣamā} + \textbf{‑isu} (verb) + \textbf{‑i} (imperative)
  \item Malayalam \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} \emph{kṣami\textbf{kkaṇaṁ}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣama} + \textbf{‑ikkuka} (verb) + \textbf{‑aṇaṁ} (necessitative)
  \item Tamil \textbf{\ta{மன்னிக்கவும்}} \emph{maṉṉi\textbf{kkavum}} — its \textbf{own} native root \emph{maṉṉi}, not Sanskrit at all
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} is a real, everyday \textquotedblleft{}sorry / please forgive me\textquotedblright{} — not stiffly formal — though in quick, casual exchanges Telugu speakers just as often reach for the borrowed English \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}sorry.\textquotedblright{}}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kṣamā\textquotedblright{} — the Sanskrit noun, forgiveness
  \item the verb — \textquotedblleft{}kṣamin̄cu,\textquotedblright{} to forgive — then \textquotedblleft{}kṣamin̄caṇḍi,\textquotedblright{} please forgive
  \item the ending you already know — \textquotedblleft{}‑aṇḍi,\textquotedblright{} same as kūrcōṇḍi
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} built from? (\textbf{Sanskrit kṣamā} + the verb-making suffix \textbf{‑in̄cu} + the respectful ending \textbf{‑aṇḍi}, which you already met on \emph{kūrcōṇḍi}.) Which cousins also verb-ify \emph{kṣamā}, and which doesn't? (\textbf{Kannada and Malayalam} do too; \textbf{Tamil} uses its own root \emph{maṉṉi}.) What's the casual alternative? (\textbf{Borrowed English \textquotedblleft{}sorry.\textquotedblright{}})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[i]{\te{ఇ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S135-letter-i}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{చ} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{౦}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ఇ}}
\textbf{\te{ఇ}} — \emph{i}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — a vowel that is a letter in its own right, not a mark hung on a consonant.

This is the pair that makes Telugu writing click. You already read \textbf{\te{◌ి}}, the \emph{i} sign: it rides on a consonant and needs one to exist. \textbf{\te{ఇ}} is the same vowel with nothing in front of it, and that is exactly when Telugu reaches for it — at the front of a word, or on a piece of a word quoted on its own.

Every vowel in this script has both forms. Meeting the pair once is worth more than meeting either alone, because from here on you can predict the rule: \textbf{sign after a consonant, letter when the vowel starts.}

You met it on the page before this one, on a suffix quoted by itself:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{‑\te{ఇంచు}} \emph{‑in̄cu} — the ending that turns a borrowed noun into a Telugu verb
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{ఇ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{ఇ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two, and say which one carries the letter \te{ఇ} and which carries the sign \te{◌ి}
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
‑\te{ఇంచు}  ·  \te{ఏమిటి}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{ఇ} three times, saying \emph{i} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{ఇ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{ఇ}? When does Telugu write the letter \te{ఇ} rather than the sign \te{◌ి}? (\textbf{When the vowel has no consonant in front of it.})

One more, from much earlier: \te{౬} — what amount does it stand for?
\end{tcolorbox}
